Signs and Wonders Movement
syns and WUN-derz MOOV-mint
noun phrase (movement)
Christian-charismatic movement initiated by John Wimber (1934-1997) at Fuller Theological Seminary's MC510 course ("Signs, Wonders, and Church Growth," 1982-1986) and at the Vineyard Christian Fellowship network. The phrase "signs and wonders" comes from Acts 2:43 et al., redeployed by Wimber and successors as a program for present-day Spirit-empowered ministry beyond the apostolic age.

Biblical Definition

The Signs and Wonders Movement is the Christian-charismatic movement initiated by John Wimber (1934-1997) at Fuller Theological Seminary in the early 1980s and centered on the Vineyard Christian Fellowship network. Wimber taught Fuller's controversial MC510 course ("Signs, Wonders, and Church Growth," 1982-1986), proposing that the present-day church should expect and pursue the signs and wonders of the apostolic age — healings, prophetic words, deliverance, sometimes raisings — as ordinary marks of Spirit-empowered ministry. The movement spread through the Vineyard network, the Toronto Blessing (1994), the Brownsville Revival (1995), and into the contemporary Bethel Church (Bill Johnson, Redding, CA) and IHOP (Mike Bickle, Kansas City) networks. Theological distinctives: present-day continuation of apostolic-age sign gifts; signs and wonders as evangelistic norm rather than apostolic accreditation; "power evangelism" over "programmatic evangelism"; expectation that physical healings should be sought and often occur in normal Christian ministry. The Reformed-confessional rebuttal is cessationist: the apostolic sign gifts (healings, miracles, prophetic word, tongues-as-foreign-language) served to accredit the apostolic foundation of the church (Heb 2:3-4; 2 Cor 12:12 "the signs of an apostle") and ceased with the close of the apostolic era and the closing of the canon (1 Cor 13:8-10). Modern claims to apostolic-level signs and wonders are tested by Scripture; documented patterns of unfulfilled prophecy, manipulated "healing", and theological drift (especially at Bethel and IHOP) confirm the cessationist concern.

Webster 1828 Definition

Christian-charismatic movement initiated by John Wimber (Fuller Seminary, 1982-86) at Vineyard; teaches present-day continuation of apostolic-age sign gifts as ordinary ministry; spread through Toronto Blessing (1994), Brownsville (1995), Bethel, IHOP; rebutted from cessationist Reformed grounds (Heb 2:3-4, 2 Cor 12:12, 1 Cor 13:8-10).

SIGNS AND WONDERS MOVEMENT, noun phrase. Christian-charismatic movement initiated by John Wimber (1934-1997).

Origin: Fuller Theological Seminary MC510 course ("Signs, Wonders, and Church Growth," 1982-1986); Vineyard Christian Fellowship network.

Subsequent expressions: Toronto Blessing (1994); Brownsville Revival (1995); Bethel Church (Bill Johnson, Redding, CA); International House of Prayer (Mike Bickle, Kansas City).

Distinctives: present-day apostolic-level sign gifts; signs-and-wonders evangelism; expectation of physical healings as ordinary ministry.

Rebutted from Reformed-confessional cessationist grounds: apostolic sign gifts served foundational accreditation and ceased with the close of the apostolic era.

Key Scripture

Hebrews 2:3-4 — "How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation; which at the first began to be spoken by the Lord, and was confirmed unto us by them that heard him; God also bearing them witness, both with signs and wonders, and with divers miracles, and gifts of the Holy Ghost, according to his own will."

2 Corinthians 12:12 — "Truly the signs of an apostle were wrought among you in all patience, in signs, and wonders, and mighty deeds."

1 Corinthians 13:8-10 — "Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away. For we know in part, and we prophesy in part. But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away."

Deuteronomy 13:1-3 — "If there arise among you a prophet, or a dreamer of dreams, and giveth thee a sign or a wonder, And the sign or the wonder come to pass... Thou shalt not hearken unto the words of that prophet, or that dreamer of dreams: for the LORD your God proveth you."

Modern Corruption

The Signs and Wonders Movement is itself the corruption pattern being named: the late-20th-century charismatic-evangelical movement claiming present-day continuation of apostolic-age sign gifts as ordinary ministry, rebutted from cessationist Reformed-confessional grounds.

expand to see more

Apostolic-accreditation framing collapsed into ordinary-ministry framing. The New Testament data on signs and wonders has a clear pattern: signs and wonders accredited the apostolic foundation of the church (Heb 2:3-4 "confirmed unto us by them that heard him... with signs and wonders"; 2 Cor 12:12 "the signs of an apostle... in signs and wonders"); they served the unique foundational moment when the apostolic message was being delivered without a closed New Testament canon to confirm it. The Reformed-confessional cessationist position holds that these sign gifts ceased with the close of the apostolic era because their function (accreditation of the apostolic foundation) was completed. The Signs and Wonders Movement collapses the foundational-accreditation function into an ordinary-ministry function, treating apostolic-level miracles as the normal expectation of every Spirit-filled congregation. The collapse is not biblical.

Empirical pattern of unfulfilled prophecy and manipulated "healing". The Signs and Wonders Movement's institutional descendants (Bethel, IHOP, the broader Vineyard) have a documented pattern of (a) prophetic words that did not come to pass (with subsequent revision or quiet abandonment), (b) "healings" that were not actual healings (medical follow-up confirms no change), and (c) theological drift on Christ's nature (Bill Johnson's Christology of Christ ministering as a man in right relationship with God), the closed canon, and biblical authority. The Reformed-confessional reader notes that Deut 13:1-3 specifically warns against following signs-and-wonders teachers who turn the people away from the LORD even when their signs come to pass; the test of a movement is conformity to Scripture, not the impressiveness of its phenomena. The empirical record of the Signs and Wonders Movement confirms what the cessationist position predicted on biblical grounds.

Hebrew Roots

Christian-charismatic movement initiated by John Wimber at Fuller Seminary (1982-86) and Vineyard; spread through Toronto Blessing (1994), Brownsville (1995), Bethel, IHOP; rebutted from cessationist Reformed-confessional grounds; signs-and-wonders served apostolic-foundation accreditation, not ordinary-ministry norm.

Founder: John Wimber (1934-1997); Fuller Theological Seminary MC510 course ("Signs, Wonders, and Church Growth," 1982-1986); Vineyard Christian Fellowship network

Subsequent expressions: Toronto Blessing (1994, at Toronto Airport Christian Fellowship); Brownsville Revival (1995, Pensacola); Bethel Church (Bill Johnson, Redding, CA); International House of Prayer (Mike Bickle, Kansas City)

Adjacent / overlapping movements: New Apostolic Reformation (q.v.); Word of Faith (q.v.); broader Third Wave charismaticism (C. Peter Wagner's term)

Reformed-confessional cessationist rebuttals: B.B. Warfield (Counterfeit Miracles, 1918, anticipates the pattern); Richard B. Gaffin Jr. (Perspectives on Pentecost, 1979); O. Palmer Robertson; Sam Waldron (To Be Continued?); Justin Peters (documentary, lecture series)

Usage

"Signs and Wonders Movement — Wimber-initiated 1980s-onward charismatic movement teaching present-day continuation of apostolic-age sign gifts as ordinary ministry."

"The signs of an apostle were wrought among you (2 Cor 12:12) — the apostolic-accreditation function that signs and wonders served and that the movement collapses into ordinary ministry."

"Cessationist Reformed-confessional position: apostolic sign gifts ceased with the close of the apostolic era; the closed canon is the rule."
